title: Cohort employment: Stable totals conceal occupational downgrading
desc: Shows automation preserved later employment while displaced incumbents suffered uneven losses, mobility and reduced career quality.

kps.k: Automation can preserve employment across successive cohorts while imposing lasting losses on displaced incumbents.
kps.d: Answering the Call of Automation contributes historical evidence rather than an AI forecast. Its telephone-dial cutover estimates distinguish decade-later outcomes for existing operators from employment among successive cohorts of young women. Incumbents lost employment and occupational standing, whereas the cohort analysis detected no overall employment decline. These findings describe different populations, not conflicting results: adjustment among later cohorts does not establish that displaced workers recovered.

kps.k: Incumbent displacement involved employment loss and occupational downgrading, with larger employment effects for older operators.
kps.d: Dial cutovers reduced the probability of remaining a telephone-industry operator a decade later by 8.1–8.7 percentage points overall. Retention losses reached 12.0–13.9 points for operators aged 26+, versus 5.0 points for those aged 16–20. Overall employment fell by 3.6–4.2 points, and movement into adjacent telephone jobs offset little of the occupational loss. Log occupation scores fell by 0.056, while the probability of declining in occupation-score decile rose by 10.1–10.5 points. These scores measure occupational outcomes, not individual wage losses.

qs.q: We initially show results for year-t operators of all ages (Columns 1 and 2), and subsequently break out effects for ages 16-20 (Columns 3 and 4), 21-25 (Columns 5 and 6), and 26+ (Columns 7 and 8).
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Stable cohort employment concealed a changed occupational mix and modest occupational downgrading.
kps.d: Among young, white, American-born women, telephone-operator employment fell by 0.66 percentage points, while overall employment estimates remained near zero and statistically insignificant. Among employed women aged 16–25, the operator share fell by 1.51 points; typist/secretary, beautician and waitress shares rose by 0.52, 0.12 and 0.81 points respectively. Log occupation scores declined by 0.010. The evidence therefore supports occupational adjustment, not unchanged job quality, and does not establish equivalent outcomes for other demographic groups.

kps.k: Geographic movement formed part of incumbent adjustment, while family-formation responses remained weak.
kps.d: Cutovers increased incumbents’ probability of moving more than 10 miles by 2.7–4.0 percentage points, with larger and clearer increases among women older than 20. Longer-distance moves also increased. Marriage estimates showed no significant overall response, and childbearing estimates offered only weak, specification-sensitive evidence. The results document relocation alongside labor-market losses; they do not establish a general shift from paid employment into family formation.

kps.k: The study informs how to assess automation’s distributional effects, but its historical design limits broader extrapolation.
kps.d: The incumbent analysis pools linked 1920–30 and 1930–40 samples, principally in cities with no more than 100,000 residents in 1920, and compares operators with matched controls. Restricting cities to continuous newspaper coverage preserves the broad negative pattern, although magnitudes and significance vary. Comparison occupations used as proxies for other technological changes show no significant cutover-associated effects. Decennial observations also mean narrow event-study bins contain different cities. The practical analytical implication is to track incumbent employment, occupational standing and mobility separately from cohort employment totals. The supplied material presents no competing-source disagreement or policy prescription, and it does not directly estimate contemporary AI displacement.

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source supports the cluster’s principal proposition with historical empirical evidence: automation’s aggregate employment effects can differ sharply from its distributional effects. It separates incumbent telephone operators from successive cohorts of young women, finding decade-later employment losses and occupational deterioration among incumbents—especially older operators—while overall employment among later cohorts remained approximately unchanged despite movement away from telephone operation and a modest decline in occupational standing. The main internal variation is therefore across populations and outcomes, not substantive disagreement: stable cohort employment coexists with incumbent displacement, migration and reduced career quality. The source also qualifies the proposition’s reach because the evidence concerns telephone dial cutovers in a historically and demographically bounded sample, estimates occupational scores rather than individual wage losses, and varies somewhat in magnitude and statistical precision across specifications. It does not directly establish comparable effects from contemporary AI. Because only one curated research source is supplied for this professional voice, this assessment characterises that source rather than academia or researchers generally.

elens.an: The source supports the proposition by providing historical empirical evidence that stable employment totals for successive cohorts can coexist with concentrated, lasting harm to workers already exposed to automation. Dial cutovers reduced decade-later employment and occupational standing among incumbent telephone operators, with larger employment losses among older incumbents. By contrast, successive cohorts of young, white, American-born women showed no detectable overall employment decline, even as telephone-operator employment contracted and workers shifted toward a different, modestly lower-scoring occupational mix. The apparent variation is therefore principally between populations and outcomes rather than evidence for and against the proposition: cohort adjustment did not imply recovery by displaced incumbents, and stable aggregate employment did not imply stable job quality. Further internal variation includes increased geographic mobility, especially among incumbents older than 20, alongside weak and inconsistent family-formation effects. The source concerns historical telephone automation rather than generative AI in 2023–2024, so it supports the proposition as an instructive precedent, not as direct evidence of contemporary AI displacement. Because the supplied period contains one curated source, no broader prevalence or cross-source consensus can be inferred.
